summary: Defines the IPv6 addressing architecture: the addressing model, the text forms used to write addresses, the kinds of unicast, anycast, and multicast addresses, and which addresses a node must recognize as its own. It was replaced by RFC 4291.

plainLanguage.summary: Every IPv6 address is 128 bits long and identifies either one interface, a set of interfaces, or a group of interfaces. This RFC defines the three kinds of address, the bit patterns that mark which kind an address is, and the short forms used to write them down.

what are the ipv6 address types
what is an ipv6 interface identifier
subtitle: How IPv6 addresses are built, how their leading bits mark the type, and how they are written down.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needed one rulebook for its addresses: what each address identifies, which kind it is, how a receiver recognises the kind, and how a person writes the address down.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three address types (unicast, anycast and multicast), gives each a fixed bit layout, and fixes the leading bits of each type so that a receiver can tell the types apart by looking at the first bits of an address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3513 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4291.

today: RFC 3513 was a Proposed Standard published in April 2003 and it obsoleted RFC 2373. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 4291.

sections.title: What IPv6 Addressing Decides
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128-bit identifiers for interfaces and sets of interfaces. There are three kinds of address. A unicast address identifies a single interface, and a packet sent to it is delivered to that interface. An anycast address identifies a set of interfaces, usually on different nodes, and a packet sent to it is delivered to the nearest one of them according to the routing protocols' measure of distance. A multicast address identifies a set of interfaces, and a packet sent to it is delivered to all of them. IPv6 has no broadcast address: multicast takes over that job.

Addresses of all types are assigned to interfaces, not to nodes. Since each interface belongs to a single node, any of that node's unicast addresses can also be used as an identifier for the node. Every interface is required to have at least one link-local unicast address, and a single interface may also have several IPv6 addresses of any type or scope. A subnet prefix is associated with one link, as in IPv4, and several subnet prefixes may be assigned to the same link.

Section 2.4 of the RFC gives the rule for recognising the type of an address from its leading bits: the unspecified address is ::/128, the loopback address is ::1/128, multicast is FF00::/8, link-local unicast is FE80::/10 and site-local unicast is FEC0::/10. Anycast addresses are taken from the unicast address space and cannot be told apart from unicast addresses by their bits. Everything that does not start with one of those prefixes must be treated as global unicast.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 address points at one network interface, at a set of interfaces, or at a group of interfaces. The first bits of the address say which kind it is, so a receiver can tell without being told.

sections.title: Writing IPv6 Addresses in Text
sections.content:
The RFC gives three conventional forms for writing an address as text. The preferred form is x:x:x:x:x:x:x:x, where each x is the hexadecimal value of one of the eight 16-bit pieces of the address, for example FEDC:BA98:7654:3210:FEDC:BA98:7654:3210. It is not necessary to write leading zeros inside a piece, but every piece must contain at least one numeral.

Because some addresses contain long strings of zero bits, a special syntax compresses them. The two characters :: indicate one or more groups of 16 bits of zeros, and :: may appear only once in an address; it can also compress leading or trailing zeros. So 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A can be written 1080::8:800:200C:417A, the multicast address FF01:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 becomes FF01::101, the loopback address becomes ::1 and the unspecified address becomes ::.

The third form suits environments that run both IPv4 and IPv6: x:x:x:x:x:x:d.d.d.d, where the six high-order pieces are hexadecimal and the last four octets are the ordinary decimal IPv4 form. The address 0:0:0:0:0:0:13.1.68.3 can then be written ::13.1.68.3.

Prefixes are written like IPv4 CIDR notation, as an address followed by a slash and the number of leftmost bits that make up the prefix, for example 12AB:0:0:CD30::/60. Leading zeros may be dropped inside a 16-bit chunk but trailing zeros may not, so 12AB:0:0:CD3/60 is not a legal way to write that prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 address is written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits. Runs of zero groups can be shortened to a double colon, which may appear only once. A prefix is the address followed by a slash and the number of bits that belong to the network.

sections.title: Unicast Addresses and Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
A global unicast address is built from a global routing prefix, a subnet ID and an interface ID. The global routing prefix is a typically hierarchical value assigned to a site, the subnet ID identifies a link within that site, and the interface ID identifies the interface on the link. Interface IDs are required to be unique within a subnet prefix, and it is recommended that the same interface ID not be assigned to different nodes on a link. Their uniqueness is independent of the uniqueness of the whole address: a global unicast address may be created with a non-global scope interface ID, and a site-local address may be created with a global scope one.

For all unicast addresses except those that start with the binary value 000, the interface ID is 64 bits long and is constructed in Modified EUI-64 format. When it is derived from a global token such as an IEEE 802 48-bit MAC address, the universal/local bit is inverted, so the bit set to one means global scope and zero means local scope. A 48-bit MAC address becomes an interface ID by inserting the two octets 0xFF and 0xFE in the middle. Where a link has no identifier of its own, as with serial links and configured tunnels, the implementation must choose an interface ID that is unique within the subnet prefix, and it should not change after a reboot or when interfaces are added or removed. A collision detection algorithm is strongly recommended as part of any automatic algorithm.

Two special addresses sit at the start of the space. The unspecified address, all zeros, must never be assigned to any node and indicates the absence of an address, as in the source address of packets sent by a host that has not yet learned its own address. It must not be used as a destination address or in a Routing header, and a router must never forward a packet whose source is the unspecified address. The loopback address, ::1, may be used by a node to send a packet to itself, must never be assigned to any physical interface, and must never leave the node.

Two kinds of local-use unicast address are defined. Link-local addresses, FE80::/10, are for use on a single link, for purposes such as automatic address configuration and neighbor discovery or when no routers are present, and routers must not forward packets with them to other links. Site-local addresses, FEC0::/10, are for use inside a single site without the need for a global prefix, and routers must not forward packets with them outside the site. Two special forms of global unicast address carry an IPv4 address in the low-order 32 bits: the IPv4-compatible address, with 0000 in that position, and the IPv4-mapped address, with FFFF there.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal IPv6 address is made of three parts: the network prefix assigned to the site, a number for the link inside it, and a number for the interface itself. The interface part is usually 64 bits and often comes from the interface's own hardware address.

sections.title: Anycast Addresses
sections.content:
An anycast address is assigned to more than one interface, typically on different nodes, and a packet sent to it is routed to the nearest interface holding that address, according to the routing protocols' measure of distance. Anycast addresses are allocated from the unicast address space using any of the defined unicast formats, so they are syntactically indistinguishable from unicast addresses. When a unicast address is assigned to more than one interface, the nodes holding it must be explicitly configured to know that it is an anycast address.

For any assigned anycast address there is a longest prefix that identifies the topological region in which all the interfaces holding that address reside. Within that region the address must be maintained as a separate entry in the routing system; outside it, the address may be aggregated into the routing entry for that prefix. In the worst case the prefix is the null prefix, so the members of the set have no topological locality and the address must be kept as a separate entry across the whole Internet, which presents a severe scaling limit on how many such global anycast sets can be supported. The RFC therefore expects support for global anycast sets to be unavailable or very restricted.

Two restrictions are imposed: an anycast address must not be used as the source address of a packet, and it must not be assigned to a host, only to a router. One anycast address is predefined and required of all routers: the Subnet-Router anycast address, formed from the subnet prefix of a link followed by fourteen zero bits. A packet sent to it is delivered to one router on that subnet, which makes it useful for an application that needs to reach any one of them.
sections.plainLanguage: An anycast address is given to several routers at once, and a packet sent to it goes to the closest one. It looks exactly like a unicast address, so the routers holding it must be told that it is shared.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses and Their Scope
sections.content:
A multicast address identifies a group of interfaces, typically on different nodes, and an interface may belong to any number of groups. Its format is 8 bits of 11111111, then 4 flag bits, then a 4-bit scope, then a 112-bit group ID. The high-order three flags are reserved and must be initialized to zero. The last flag, T, says whether the group is permanently assigned, meaning well-known and assigned by IANA when T is 0, or transient, meaning not permanently assigned, when T is 1.

The scope field limits how far a multicast group reaches. The assigned values are 1 interface-local, which spans a single interface on a node and is useful only for loopback transmission; 2 link-local; 4 admin-local, the smallest scope that must be configured by an administrator; 5 site-local; 8 organization-local, for several sites of one organization; and E global. The values 0 and F are reserved, and the remaining values are unassigned and available for administrators to define regions.

The meaning of a permanently assigned address does not depend on the scope. If the NTP servers group has the group ID 101, then FF01:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 means the NTP servers on the same interface as the sender, FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 the ones on the same link, FF05:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 the ones in the same site, and FF0E:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 the ones in the Internet. A transient address means nothing outside the scope it was created in.

Several multicast addresses are predefined. FF01:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 and FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 identify all IPv6 nodes within scope 1 or 2. FF01:0:0:0:0:0:0:2, FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:2 and FF05:0:0:0:0:0:0:2 identify all IPv6 routers within scope 1, 2 or 5. The solicited-node address FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FFXX:XXXX is computed from a node's own addresses: take the low-order 24 bits of a unicast or anycast address and append them to the prefix FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FF00::/104. A node must compute and join the solicited-node address for every unicast and anycast address it is assigned, so addresses that differ only in their high-order bits share one multicast address. Multicast addresses must not be used as source addresses or appear in a Routing header, and routers must not forward multicast packets beyond the scope in the destination address.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast address names a group of interfaces. The scope field in the address says how far the group reaches, from one interface up to the whole Internet, and the group ID says which group it is inside that scope.

sections.title: The Addresses a Node Must Recognize
sections.content:
A host is required to recognize the following addresses as identifying itself: its required link-local address for each interface, any additional unicast and anycast addresses configured for the node's interfaces, the loopback address, the all-nodes multicast addresses, the solicited-node multicast address for each of its unicast and anycast addresses, and the multicast addresses of all other groups to which the node belongs.

A router is required to recognize all the addresses that a host must recognize, plus the Subnet-Router anycast addresses for all interfaces for which it is configured to act as a router, all other anycast addresses with which the router has been configured, and the all-routers multicast addresses.

The RFC also states its position on security: IPv6 addressing documents do not have any direct impact on Internet infrastructure security, and authentication of IPv6 packets is defined elsewhere. Section 4 of the RFC replaces the previous assignment of IPv6 address space, allocating the binary prefix 001, one eighth of the space, to global unicast addresses and leaving about 85 percent of the space unassigned for future definition and use.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host must recognize the addresses that belong to it, so that packets sent to any of them are accepted. A router must also recognize the anycast and multicast addresses meant for routers.

viz.caption: HOW THE TYPE OF AN IPV6 ADDRESS IS RECOGNIZED

items.label: Global unicast
items.desc: Any address that does not start with one of the prefixes above.

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: Eight bits of 11111111 identify the address as multicast.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Three reserved bits set to zero and the T flag: 0 for a permanently assigned group, 1 for a transient group.

fields.name: Scope
fields.desc: Limits the group: 1 interface-local, 2 link-local, 4 admin-local, 5 site-local, 8 organization-local, E global.

fields.name: Group ID
fields.desc: Identifies the multicast group within the given scope.
